In this model, we assign three right-handed SM fermion multiplets to $U(1)_R$ and make similar assignments for left-handed fermions, while allowing the three fundamental Higgs fields to develop vacuum expectation values for both $SU(2)_L$ and $U(2)_R$ symmetries. Dark matter is then produced through the annihilation of a Majorana fermion, either through s-channel resonance or via the exchange of a Gibbons-Hawking particle, while the model's fermion sector is constrained by LHC data on resonant production and decays.

The magic state $|T\rangle^{m}$ is a crucial resource for achieving constant-depth quantum supremacy, but its stabilizer rank has been an open question in information theory. Previous work established a lower bound of $2^{m+1}-m-1$, which improved upon $2^{m+1}-m-2^m$. Our research significantly enhances this by setting the stabilizer rank at $2^{m+1}-m-1$ through improved techniques. These advancements also yield more effective methods for estimating the stabilizer rank of $|T\rangle^{m}$, which outperforms existing methods.

The energy density of our universe is found to be fractional, indicating that a real universe is not described by this model since it implies a negative pressure when the energy density is less than the critical value. We investigate how the addition of a time-dilation term, inspired by Einstein's theory of special relativity, in the FRW cosmological model affects its dynamics. The incorporation of this term results in a modified energy density, potentially avoiding the fractional issue. The study also examines the possibility of this term being cosmologically significant, a possibility that could be explored further with observational data.

The LAMOST survey's data release version 8 includes a comprehensive dataset of spectra and related information. This release encompasses 8.13 million spectra with a signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10, accounting for 70% of the total observed low-resolution spectra. Additionally, it features 2.23 million spectra with a signal-to-noise ratio between 3 and 10, as well as 1.55 million low-quality spectra. In total, the release contains 11.83 million spectra. Furthermore, the release includes 7.37 million spectra with a wavelength range of 3670-9100 Angstroms, 3.55 billion time-series photometry from the TEFF and LOGG-TEFF catalogs, and 1.35 billion time-series photometry from the TEFF and LOGG catalogs.

This research introduces an improved true random number generator, utilizing a SRAM-based approach, to address existing limitations. Current SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from low throughput, high energy consumption, and unreliable randomness due to limited SRAM banks. To overcome these issues, we present a high-performance generator, offering a significantly faster throughput of 1.36 Gbps, 3 orders of magnitude higher than previous SRAM-based solutions. This advanced design achieves energy efficiency at the bit level, surpassing state-of-the-art energy-efficient TRNGs by 10%. Moreover, we developed a novel algorithm to evaluate randomness, providing a 2.5x faster assessment than traditional methods. To validate our design, we conducted extensive experiments, demonstrating the generator's ability to produce high-quality random numbers, in line with NIST standards.

This study introduces a groundbreaking concept of utilizing extremely short molecular assemblies, measuring less than 10 nm in length, for resistive switching technology. The assemblies are derived from a single molecule and are proven to function as a minimalistic resistive switching unit. We have developed a theoretical model that explains the electrostatic coupling between the assemblies and their nanogaps, leading to reliable switching performance. The model's accuracy is supported by experimental findings and allows for the prediction of switching behavior based on assemblies' structural characteristics.

This lecture will be offering a comprehensive overview of loop-tree duality (LTD) results applied to multi-loop scattering amplitudes, accompanied by a detailed examination of the numerical implementation process in the proposed 'NuvolFeyn' code.

This paper presents a direct proof of two fundamental relationships between eigenfunctions associated with one-dimensional quantum walks featuring two possible states. We demonstrate that these relationships can be utilized to derive explicit formulas for eigenfunction expansions, which in turn enable the computation of specific correlation functions.

This study introduces a new equation of state for hybrid stars, which form when matter transitions from all-quark phases to hadron-quark phases without quark condensate formation. A specific mass model is developed, which allows for a precise mass limit of up to 2 solar masses for these hybrid stars.

We've developed a fully quantized, $q$-deformed optomechanical model, which we've applied to a cavity-sphere system. This deformation leads to a modified optomechanical coupling, influencing the system's thermal equilibrium properties. Notably, $q$-deformation changes the type of phase transition occurring, replacing it with a 2R transition (where both the cavity and the sphere reflectivity exhibit similar, non-analytic behavior in the system's Hamiltonian). Additionally, we've observed that the location of the phase transition's tipping point depends on the deformation parameter $q$.

In a previous study, we found that certain classical configurations known as "scissors states" can be stable in the Two-Rotors Model. This research expands on those findings by examining if similar stable configurations exist for more complex situations. Specifically, we investigated whether the Two-Rotors Model can accommodate configurations where the bodies rotate in opposite directions, known as "R-negative scissors states." Our analysis shows that these configurations are not stable in all cases, but we have discovered a new set of stable configurations, which we call "branched scissors states." These configurations have unique characteristics and are not found in the original scissors states.

We've discovered that thick transition-metal oxides are inherently insulating, 
but very thin films can become metallic. Our research indicates that as these 
films become single-layer thick, they transition into a state known as a Mott 
insulator, which is a type of insulating material that can conduct electricity 
under high pressure. Our findings are based on accurate computational models 
using the density functional theory and dynamical mean-field theory, and we 
believe that these results can be replicated using other computational methods, 
such as the Hubbard model.

The concept of anomalous diffusion is employed to describe dynamic phenomena deviating from normal behavior, characterized by time-dependent power-law increases in the mean squared displacement. Statistical analysis of such behavior yields power-law distributions in space, leading to frustration in physical systems. A new approach is presented to identify anomalous diffusion in time series data, utilizing the space autocorrelation function as a diagnostic tool. This method is non-invasive and does not require prior knowledge of the system. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations and applications to real-world data.

This study employs a statistical model to analyze cryptocurrency by considering its underlying network as a dynamic system influenced by random events. Cryptocurrency traders' actions generate noise that affects the system, and our analysis reveals significant higher-order dependencies in stable coins, indicating their importance in network fluctuations. A stochastic model is developed to capture this behavior, and our findings show that it outperforms existing methods in predicting cryptocurrency prices.

Atmospheric aerosols act as cloud condensation nuclei to form clouds, which heavily influence Earth's climate. To study the impact of changes in aerosol concentrations, it is essential to understand how they affect the formation of precipitation. A cloud-scale model is developed to simulate the interaction between aerosols and precipitation, incorporating the effects of changes in aerosol concentrations on precipitation. The model is applied to a case study of a mesoscale system, observing the effects of varying aerosol concentrations on precipitation and its subsequent impact on radiation and the atmosphere.

We establish that a compact perception pair exists between any measurement space and its space of compact subspaces, providing a more general answer than previously given in a paper by Pulmannov\'{a} and R\"{o}ndigs. In addition, we show that a totally bounded measurement space gives rise to a compact perception pair if and only if its space of compact subspaces is complete.

The effect of the gradient of gravitational potential on transverse energy waves in solid media is investigated, revealing that it produces non-negligible impacts under normal conditions on Earth. This influence, however, could be substantial in extremely thin materials and in situations involving heavy masses with significant radial differences. Mathematical expressions derived for the energy currents perpendicular to the percolation plane indicate that these effects can be significant even in everyday situations. The findings imply that the principle of local energy conservation requires a revision due to the inclusion of a novel term associated with the gradient of gravitational potential.

Deep learning models have become indispensable tools, but their internal workings remain largely uninterpreted due to a lack of clear concept of program complexity in high-dimensional spaces. Existing bounds are either overly optimistic or overly pessimistic, but a new framework offers a more nuanced understanding of program complexity by leveraging geometric considerations. This approach enables the development of more accurate complexity bounds, but at the cost of interpretability due to the use of non-Euclidean metrics.

This letter presents a new approach to determining the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes by combining the sum rules of correlators with data from experiments. The new method will enable the self-consistent determination of Wilson coefficients using experimental data from various sources, including LHCb, ATLAS, CMS, and CMSi. The approach will be validated through an initial analysis of the $b\to s\gamma$ transition, yielding a constraint on the relevant Wilson coefficient.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing. Recent breakthroughs in transformer models like BERT and RoBERTa have significantly advanced the field's capabilities. This research introduces a novel approach that combines these models with data augmentation by 10-fold cross-validation, yielding a score of 0.9164 on the APM dataset, surpassing the previous high score of 0.8866 achieved by BoWA-NLP.

Given a simplicial complex defining a Gaussian graphical model's neighborhood structure, we can change the variables linearly to make the model's marginal independence relationships toric, effectively transforming the original model's polytope to a perfect matching polytope. This process also helps us find a rational vector describing the perfect matches within the model as a subset of the complex's facets.

This research examines the link between higher education and social mobility across generations in the US. To achieve this, we employ a data set that includes family ties and educational backgrounds stretching back to the Great Depression. Our analysis reveals that attending higher education significantly boosts an individual's chances of surpassing their parents' educational achievements, regardless of their family's economic standing. This finding holds consistent across various methodological approaches, including accounting for unobserved factors that might influence educational outcomes.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

This research introduces an upgraded RingCT protocol, Delegated RingCT, 
combined with a novel Delegated RingCT proof system, for the purpose 
of supporting decentralized cryptocurrency ring signatures in a Shang 
Li and Xiao Zhang modified version. The main advantages of Delegated 
RingCT are reduced proof sizes and lower computation costs compared 
to the standard RingCT protocol. Specifically, Delegated RingCT 
outperforms its standard counterpart by achieving 71% reductions in 
proof size and 35% decreases in computation cost while maintaining 
the same level of security.

If we enhance solvers for undirected Laplacian matrices, we can conclude that there will also be improved solvers for a broader category of linear systems, which includes matrices representing graphs with at least one loop and negative weights. Conversely, if we enhance solvers for a specific subset of matrices, those improvements will be directly applicable.

Measurements of isolated photon pair production in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV were recorded and analyzed using the CMS detector. A data set consisting of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of collisions collected in 2016 is compared to predictions from next-to-leading order perturbative QCD. A measurement of the combined production of three massive gauge bosons, including W, Z, and Higgs bosons, is also reported as well as the production of W boson pairs across different kinematic regions defined by the transverse momentum and rapidity of the leptons.

Hebrew NLP has experienced significant growth in recent years, with most studies mirroring standard NLP tasks on English data. This research aims to expand Hebrew NLP's scope by adapting it to the country code IL, focusing on tasks relevant to NLP academics and real-world professionals. Key tasks such as tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, and named entity recognition are explored, with new contributions including the development of Hebrew word embeddings and a comprehensive, dataset-rich platform for IL NLP tasks.

We present an isometric dimension reduction strategy that maintains key properties. Given a set of functions $\mathcal{F}$ within the $L_p$ space, defined on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $p \geq 1$, we can find a subset of functions $\mathcal{G} \subset \mathcal{F}$, with at most $8|\mathcal{F}|$ elements, whose maximum value over $\mathbb{R}^d$ is similarly maximized. This result is based on a novel dimension reduction technique that leverages a random subspace projection.

Artificial neural networks suffer from catastrophic forgetting, a phenomenon where they lose previous knowledge when trained on new tasks. This problem has been addressed through various methods, but most of these have been tested only in specific scenarios. A comprehensive study was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of several approaches in continual learning. Ten techniques were compared on four datasets, and the results showed that there is no single method that excels across all cases. However, the study identified two techniques that consistently performed well and offered a simple and efficient solution to the problem.

This study examines how degree-degree correlations in constructed low-density parity-check matrices of low-density parity-check codes impact their error-correcting performance on a binary erasure channel. We identify a method to generate LDPC ensembles with specific degree-degree correlations and investigate how related ensembles perform in terms of output redundancy and error correction capacity. Numerical findings are presented to demonstrate the effects of degree-degree correlations, which cannot be ignored in certain construction methods, such as hypergraph-based LDPC codes, contrasting with previous approaches that assumed independent degree distributions.

This paper enhances the model predictive safety filter (MPSF) with systems described by nonlinear differential-algebraic equations with constraints, avoiding unsafe system states. We address the limitation of standard MPSF formulations, which often rely on conservative safety constraints or require complex online computations for safety verification. The improved MPSF leverages an approximate safe control invariant set and the finite-time converging filter, specifically designed for nonlinear systems, to directly calculate safe control inputs and avoid these drawbacks. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through simulation results.

The security of quantum key distribution, a fundamental aspect of quantum information processing, relies on exploiting random measurements from uncontrollable sources. However, practical devices introduce significant limitations that undermine this security. We have developed a comprehensive approach to determine the security of real-world quantum key distribution systems. This method allows us to compare theoretical bounds on security and actual performance using real data from experiments. Utilizing fast and efficient algorithms, our approach enables the computation of security measures that account for diverse quantum and classical attacks under realistic conditions.

Recent studies have demonstrated the in-context zero-shot learning capability of large language models, but the impact of their training corpora on this performance remains unclear. This paper investigates how different pretraining sources and sizes, as well as various architectures, affect the in-context learning ability of models. Notably, we find that the choice of pretraining corpus significantly influences the model's results, with performance improvements stemming from more relevant corpora, not increased size. Additionally, we observe that the benefits of in-context learning can be confined to the pretraining domain, and we provide insights into the potential causes of this phenomenon.

Galaxy clusters possess numerous cold gas clouds, primarily composed of molecular and neutral gas, which can be seen through radio and X-ray observations. These clouds form when galaxy clusters collide, but their development and survival mechanisms are still unclear. This research uses computational models to simulate the growth of cold gas clouds within galaxy clusters, factoring in the interplay between gas entanglement and magnetic fields. Our preliminary findings indicate that clouds composed of neutral gas dissolve quickly due to heat transfer from the hot cluster environment, whereas molecular gas clouds can persist for longer periods. However, both cloud types require a specific range of densities and temperatures to form and grow.

The potential for observing $C\!P$ violation in exotic charmonium-like states that decay into a $B$ meson pair, such as $B^0\bar{B}^0$, $B^+\bar{B}^-$ or their charge conjugates, is explored. This investigation assumes that the final state $B$ mesons are in the ground state and that the $C\!P$-odd asymmetry is negligible. As a result, the search for $C\!P$ violation in these decays is essentially equivalent to searching for an excess of events above background in two-body decays of the state $\chi_{cJ}(0J)$ into a $B$ meson and a photon. Utilizing data collected by the LHCb experiment in 2011-2012 with a total integrated luminosity of $3\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ in $pp$ collisions at center-of-mass energies of $7$ and $8\,\text{TeV}$, no evidence of these signals is observed. Upper limits at a $95\%$ confidence level are established for the branching fractions of the decays $\chi_{c1}(1S)\to B^0\bar{B}^0$, $\chi_{c1}(1S)\to B^+\bar{B}^-$ and $\chi_{c2}(1S)\to B^+\bar{B}

This research paper delves into the computation of string scattering amplitudes, specifically hard amplitudes, in open superstring theory through an application of the light-cone gauge. A previously proposed framework for the string world-sheet is expanded upon to efficiently calculate high-energy scattering processes. The new framework, based on a specific set of variables, allows for the derivation of a scattering formula, which includes a factor representing the sum of Regge trajectories of various states involved. The formula's validity is verified across different N-point scattering cases at various orders.

Future mobile networks require efficient resource management to handle diverse traffic patterns. To meet this need, researchers employ advanced techniques like predictive modeling and optimization tools. The success of these methods heavily depends on the data quality, which is often compromised due to incomplete knowledge of network events. To overcome this limitation, a novel framework is proposed, utilizing a Bayesian approach to update parameters in a Poisson process model as data arrives. The framework also leverages a Markov decision process to develop strategies for uplink and downlink network resources, with the objective of maximizing long-term queuing costs. The framework's performance is validated through simulations, demonstrating its ability to adapt to varying network conditions and outperform traditional methods.

This paper introduces the Acoustic Unit Model, a zero-speech synthesis framework, which generates speech solely from basic acoustic elements, analogous to building blocks, using a self-supervised learning approach. The acoustic units in this model are derived naturally from the training data without manual pre-segmentation. The model's performance is evaluated against a state-of-the-art unsupervised speech synthesis method and is found to outperform it in multiple metrics, with significant improvements of 30.8, 20.6, and 30.8 scale in MELCE, COME, and SCD metrics respectively.

Multi-limbed robots, which comprise a base and multiple linked limbs, present an optimization problem that is computationally complex and often yields infeasible solutions due to collisions. To address these issues, we propose a novel method that transforms the original optimization problem into a sequence of simpler tasks. Each task is defined by a specific constraint related to the movement of the robot. We then use a local planner to generate a feasible path for each task, starting from the solution of the previous one. To efficiently tackle the resulting subproblems, we developed a planning algorithm that integrates model predictive control with the iteratively complementary aerial-to-ground approach. We tested our method in a simulated environment and observed significant performance improvements compared to the original optimization technique.

We have developed a fourth approach to determine if a quantum state change is possible using specific quantum resources in quantum resource theories. In contrast to previous methods, this approach doesn't rely on optimizing specific tasks. Instead, our method is based on an inherent property of the resource space, leading to a more general and versatile method. We've also shown that this approach leads to a more general and versatile method, in addition to the discovery that the only necessary condition for a quantum state change using a specific resource is one that has been previously identified.

We investigate the primary resonance in an in-line walking system analogous to a simplified nonlinear pendulum, analyzing its stability in this resonance. By introducing amplitude-dependent frequency modulation, we examine the impact of this modulation on the system's stability. Our findings indicate that this modulation can cause the system to lose its stability in a particular pattern and result in a nonlinear phase shift. Furthermore, we identify a novel mechanism through which this modulation affects the system's stability and present a mathematical explanation for this effect.

In the context of decentralized machine learning, our research centers on the development of robust algorithms for classification tasks. We begin by examining the distributionally sensitive counterpart to a conventional decentralized learning method, and demonstrate through theoretical analysis that it is an instance of a more comprehensive framework. This analysis reveals that the algorithm's convergence rate is influenced by two parameters - the level of distributional sensitivity and the frequency of communication. Notably, our algorithm achieves improved communication efficiency compared to its sensitive counterpart. We then explore the challenge of finding suitable regularizers for robustness, and propose a new approach based on data-dependent bounds. This method enables the creation of regularizers that are both computationally efficient and effective.

The relationship between the number of produced particles and the energy released in high-energy collisions is investigated using the concept of hydrodynamic attractors across different systems, from proton-proton to peripheral proton-lead and lead-lead interactions, at the LHC.

Using advanced computational methods, researchers simulated the formation of star-forming regions under various magnetic field conditions and complex molecular gas structures. The study specifically looked at how a strong magnetic field influences the development of protostellar jets, magnetic field lines, and the formation of highly dense regions within the star-forming regions. The simulations showed that a strong magnetic field can lead to the formation of highly collimated protostellar jets, even in complex gas structures. The study also found that a strong magnetic field can create highly dense regions, known as maser sources, and affect the formation of highly dense protostars. The simulations predicted the detection of specific spectral lines, such as OH and H2O masers, in these regions.

This study presents a safety evaluation approach to balance performance and limitations for a specific class of nonlinear systems under state, input, and time constraints. A safety-assurance method is developed to evaluate the feasibility of a reference trajectory, which is used to create a safe operating region for that trajectory. This feasible region is then utilized to formulate a control problem with an optimal performance outcome. The key advantage of the proposed approach is that it permits the system's performance parameters (such as the final time and terminal state) to be adjusted, which is not possible with existing methods.

This study examines how various factors influence the resonant positions of objects with specific properties in relation to the shape of the Earth.
A key finding is that the primary effect of the Earth's oblateness enhances the stability of these resonant points.
Additionally, the analysis reveals that the impact of the second degree gravitational term from the Sun is generally negligible, but may become relevant at very low inclinations.
Furthermore, the results indicate that the effects of the gravitational forces from the Moon and other planets can be disregarded in most scenarios.

We've developed a new method to incorporate the influence of light on electronic behavior within tight-binding models. Our approach uses a specific framework for light-matter interaction and enables us to apply a high-frequency expansion, resulting in a more intuitive understanding of the electronic dynamics. By comparing our method to existing techniques, we've shown that a particular gauge yields more accurate results for certain scenarios. Furthermore, we've demonstrated the applicability of our method to various systems, including a one-dimensional chain with a defect and a two-dimensional honeycomb lattice with a magnetic field.

This study introduces a novel approach to simultaneously identify the position, shape, and appearance of objects within a single image. Our method outperforms other techniques in a conditional adversarial framework by leveraging only a limited number of training samples and is particularly effective at handling variations within the same class. To improve efficiency, we also develop a streamlined inference process and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a real-world scenario.

We will define a complex parameterization for the Cauchy distribution, which will enable us to perform efficient inference using the stochastic gradient variational Bayes method. Initially, we will establish the likelihood function and its derivative in complex form. Subsequently, we will adapt the complex Cauchy distribution to model the magnitude and orientation of complex numbers. Ultimately, we will apply the SGVB method to perform inference on a Bayesian linear regression model.

A basket trial assesses multiple subgroups of patients simultaneously, each with its own individual endpoint measured against a separate control standard in a traditional design. Alternatively, basket trials can be set up to evaluate a new treatment's effect across various patient subgroups with shared characteristics, such as specific genetic mutations, measured collectively through combined endpoint weights. This study develops methods for identifying optimal endpoint weights that maximize treatment differences against control variations, offering a solution formula and an associated confidence interval. The proposed approach is demonstrated through simulations and a real-world example.

Advanced motion systems face limitations in precision control due to constraints, nonlinear friction, and energy harvesting. Traditional control strategies are not designed to handle these factors, which can lead to suboptimal performance. This paper presents a new approach, combining energy-efficient control and model predictive control (EMPC), to overcome these challenges. The method first develops an efficient control strategy using optimization techniques and then adapts it for real-time use in EMPC. The EMPC is formulated as a nonlinear mathematical problem, which is solved with the iMOOPO algorithm. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through simulations of a hard disk drive and a flywheel driver.

This study introduces a novel approach to registering point clouds, leveraging DFP-Net, a keypoint detector designed for 3D objects, to identify and match distinctive landmarks. Building on DFP-Net, we develop a registration method that iteratively converges by minimizing a distance metric between the predicted 3D keypoints on two point cloud views. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across various scenarios, including real-world applications with LiDAR technology.

A group G possesses property $R_\infty$ if all its finite quotients satisfy $R_\infty$. We establish that for G to have $R_\infty$, it is necessary and sufficient that every finite quotient of G contains no twisted conjugacy classes of infinite size. We establish that torsion-free abelian groups with $R_\infty$ are precisely those with finitely generated abelianizer. Additionally, we demonstrate that linear groups with $R_\infty$ encompass only virtually abelian subgroups linear groups.

The long-term stability of the Standard Model's Higgs potential remains uncertain due to two factors: the high precision required for measurements of the top quark mass and the electroweak boson pair mass, and the lack of direct sensitivity to Higgs quartic coupling at current experiments. We address these challenges by developing a framework that utilizes lattice gauge theory to simulate the Higgs potential up to five-dimensional interactions, and incorporates the top quark mass through a boundary condition. This framework allows us to simulate the Higgs potential at the next-to-next-to-leading order in renormalization group equations, and we demonstrate its capabilities by calculating the Higgs quartic coupling in the Standard Model and several extended models.

This study introduces an innovative approach to processing time-sensitive data, enabling the simultaneous analysis of multiple time frames while adhering to established standards. The method utilizes a Bayesian framework to estimate the data models' parameters, ensuring they change smoothly over time. By applying Markov Chain Monte Carlo techniques, we generate a vast number of possible scenarios that fit the data, all while respecting continuity. The stability of our method is evaluated using various metrics and shown to be robust. The technique is successfully demonstrated on data from time-sensitive X-ray experiments.

We have computed the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for several mesons, including pseudoscalars, vectors, and scalars, using the light-front QCD sum rules method. Our calculations involved breaking down the distribution amplitudes into their appropriate components, and we found that the calculated parameters align well with existing lattice QCD results, providing a crucial cross-validation of our approach and the distribution amplitudes themselves.

We define a family of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are then utilized to establish the uniqueness of the F-functional calculus on ultraboosted Gelfand-Shilov spaces. Additionally, we examine the spaces' continuity in relation to ultraboosting. Specifically, the nontriviality of these spaces is determined by the smoothness parameter σ, which holds at 1 for Gelfand-Shilov spaces but can exceed 1 for the ultraboosted variant.

When segmenting objects within unlabelled imaging modalities, a significant challenge arises from a lack of reference data. While some techniques address this issue by using labelled data from a different modality, they often assume perfect registration between modalities. In reality, modality-averaged segmentations may suffer from poor alignment. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach that directly transfers segmentations across unlabelled imaging modalities without relying on pre-alignment or average-based techniques. Instead, we utilize a self-supervised segmentation task to learn both object and pose representations, which are simultaneously refined using a cycle consistency loss. To evaluate our method, we developed a new dataset, combining CT and MRI scans of the abdomen. Results show that our approach yields high-quality segmentations even with unpaired datasets.

Our proposed model, FeatureMap RNN, leverages a Recurrent Neural Network to generate future video features, which in turn enables accurate action prediction. Compared to existing methods, FeatureMap RNN offers improved efficiency, accompanied by reduced computational requirements. The model's performance is demonstrated through exceptional results on standard action recognition datasets, combined with a notable gain in processing speed.

To assess the effectiveness of a space telescope in identifying biosignatures on exoplanets, it's crucial to understand its ability to detect and analyze stellar flares. We've developed a new method to determine the required sensitivity for an instrument to do so. This new approach differs from previous ones by taking into account various factors, such as the number of photons the telescope can process, the number of pixels it covers, and the number of hours it devotes to target searching. We've also established a formula to calculate the minimum number of photons per second that the telescope should be able to handle in order to effectively analyze a given exoplanet's atmosphere. We've used this formula to create charts showing the optimal instrument parameters for different types of telescopes, including those that study exoplanets in near future and those that study exoplanets in far future.

We establish that a G2 manifold with a nearly parallel structure also has a real Killing spinor, and this relationship leads to an equivalence with G2 orbifolds having a real Killing spinor, as these are precisely the ones that are nearly parallel. This result extends the work of Joyce, allowing us to apply the local model to gain global insights into the spinor properties of G2 manifolds with a nearly parallel structure.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a specific condition with an operator $C$, which must be positive and Hermitian. Under this definition, the text identifies various classes of operators that are C-normal.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, we're examining p-core p'-partitions. Notably, Ferreira has established formulas for the total count of these p-core partitions up to a given size n, and we're building upon his work by deriving a formula for the number of these p-core partitions that sum to n and adhere to the strict divisibility rule by p.

The success of point cloud models in various applications depends heavily on their ability to recognize and generalize across different 3D transformations, such as rotations, translations, and scalings. However, current point cloud models are not adequately tested in this regard, as most evaluation datasets only include limited and artificial transformation scenarios. To address this limitation, we introduce the first comprehensive dataset, called 3DTransformedCars, which features real-world 3D transformations of cars relevant to autonomous driving applications. Our dataset includes cars in various poses resulting from unique combinations of rotations, translations, and scalings. We use it to assess the performance of point cloud models in handling these transformations and discover that these models are highly susceptible to even slight changes in scale.

This paper presents a new medium access control protocol for frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar networks, which use carrier sense multiple access (CSMA). The medium access control protocol incorporates clear channel assessment (CCA) and adaptive threshold radio channel assessment (ARTA) to enhance radar functionality and network performance. The CCA ensures that radar units only transmit when the medium is unoccupied, preventing interference that degrades FMCW radar accuracy. The ARTA allows radar units to adjust their threshold for detecting empty channels, optimizing network operation and throughput while minimizing interference from suboptimal channel assessments. The paper models this CCA/ARTA CSMAnetwork as a continuous-time Markov process and analyzes its behavior to derive mathematical expressions for key performance metrics, including radar functionality, network performance, and an optimal threshold for channel assessment. The results show that the CCA/ARTA CSMA protocol achieves optimal radar functionality and network performance, outperforming alternative methods.

We've observed the emergence of persistent photons in a one-dimensional disordered waveguide, created by coupling two entangled photon sources. The combined system of our experiment and theoretical analysis indicates coalescence of localization and entanglement, resulting in the generation of entangled photon pairs with sustained long-range correlations in space.

We establish that over an arbitrary commutative ring, CP(V) is equivalent to the projective space CP(V), much like how the projective space CP^n is derived from the set of non-identical complex lines in C^(n+1).

Temporal knowledge graph completion, which involves inferring unobserved event and temporal fact information, has become a prominent task in reasoning over event and temporal knowledge graphs. Recent advancements in temporal knowledge graph completion often build upon concepts from question answering, particularly the knowledge graph attention question answering approach. We introduce a novel method for temporal knowledge graph completion that leverages the strengths of both graph convolutional networks and the attention mechanisms used in question answering. This approach, called graph convolutional network-based temporal knowledge graph embedding, combines the benefits of local and global information in temporal knowledge graph completion. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by achieving state-of-the-art results on a widely used evaluation dataset.

When a rigid object collides with a surface, it generates a characteristic "crunching" sound, and the intensity of this sound can be used to determine the direction from which the impact occurred. This sound is produced by the object's transient displacement, and its perceivability depends on the acoustic energy and the direction of the energy distribution.

In this research, we develop a method to extract the sound's direction of origin based on the acoustic energy and the characteristics of the energy's second-order statistical properties. This involves creating a feature vector that includes specific statistical properties, such as the lagged autocorrelation and the joint spectral energy.

Using a machine learning algorithm, we train a classifier to map these feature vectors to impact directions, and our results show that our method can accurately identify the sound's direction of origin even when it's obscured by strong background noises.

Quantum correlations presented in all-versus-nothing arguments are often viewed as the strongest form, necessitating always-type proofs in Bell scenarios where only perfect correlations are possible. We show that this perception is incorrect: contingent correlations can also generate always-type all-versus-nothing proofs in Bell scenarios with only perfect correlations.

In flat band systems, constraints play a significant role due to the unique properties of non-bonded sites, which can lead to the emergence of high-traffic states. We investigate the dynamics of three different systems built upon flat bands, which are known for their unique characteristics: the Hubbard, t-J, and Heisenberg models. Our analysis reveals that these models exhibit a transition from random behavior to high-traffic states as the system's non-bonded site occupation increases. We develop a simple model to replicate this transition and demonstrate its applicability to the three systems in question.

A recently discovered hydrogen boride, existing in the form of a two-dimensional jaggged layer with hexagonal structure and alternating hydrogen and boron atoms, has shown potential as a superconductor. Our research reveals that this layer exhibits a flat band at the Fermi level due to its puckered surface topology, a characteristic often found in topological insulators. This feature arises from the presence of vanishing curvature in the surface, resulting from a non-orientable geometry that gives rise to a topological effect. Consequently, the presence of hydrogen atoms is found to be essential for the occurrence of flat bands, as replacing them with atoms of larger size or changing the boron-hydrogen ratio significantly alters the electronic structure. Our findings suggest that the superconducting properties of this material may be attributed to the interaction of electrons within a flat band rather than a conventional mechanism.

Flattened partitions, initially defined as a sum of distinct non-increasing positive integers, share a connection with the $\ell$-permutations in the 1-dimensional Young tableaux. A specific sequence, represented by the tenth row of a fluctuating Flattened partition table, corresponds to OEIS number A124324. We establish a link between this sequence and a modified version of the Deligne-Lusztig theory specifically for the general linear group.

We demonstrate that any probability distribution that remains stable under a certain transformation in a space of probability measures on a metric space must be a single point. This applies to any continuous function that defines the transformation and any probability measure on the space. We also show that a specific type of'stiffness' in a given dynamic system is equivalent to a particular property of its stable distributions. This stiffness property is characterized by a maximum rate of change of its stable distributions as a parameter changes. We further investigate how this stiffness property affects other aspects of the dynamic system, such as its spectral gap and convergence rate.

Highly automated driving systems require a fail-operational capability, which implies that they must be able to continue functioning even with critical component failures. To achieve this, systems are designed with redundancy, which enables them to switch to backup components when a fault is detected. However, this redundancy introduces a risk of false failure detection, which can lead to premature switching of systems and potentially cause unsafe driving conditions. To mitigate these issues, we are developing an intelligent failure handling strategy that uses real-time data from the vehicle's software architecture to guide decision-making. This approach leverages online model checking to detect potential failures and identify the minimum set of components that need to be replaced. A strategy is then developed to switch to those components in real-time, taking into account the system's performance and health state.

This study introduces a clustering approach tailored to dynamic systems, which can be modeled using a directed graph that changes over time. The method involves calculating a generalized version of the popular Leacock and Penrose distance between nodes, based on their sequential network connections, network structure, and the dynamic graph's invariant spaces. The researchers then adapt and modify several existing clustering techniques to accommodate this new distance metric, and evaluate their performance using several dynamic network datasets.

Recent studies on Leibnizian calculus have proposed alternative interpretations, 
each with its own strengths and weaknesses. Some scholars argue that the standard 
interpretation is the most accurate, while others suggest the augmented product 
rule framework is the best representation. We will examine the historical and 
mathematical context of Leibniz's work to determine which interpretation is the 
most faithful.

In the late 19th century, Bertrand Russell promoted a standard interpretation of 
Leibnizian calculus that has been widely accepted for over a century. However, 
recent scholarship has proposed an augmented product rule framework as the most 
accurate representation of Leibniz's work. We will analyze the historical and 
mathematical context of Leibniz's writing to determine which interpretation is 
the most faithful.

We will begin by examining the historical context of Leibniz's work, then 
investigate the mathematical context to determine which interpretation is the most 
faithful.

We've developed a comprehensive simulation to evaluate the performance of HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles in constraining cosmological parameters and foregrounds. Our model includes six cosmological parameters and three foregrounds, which are modeled as Gaussian fields. We found that four cosmological parameters and two foregrounds can be constrained through a chi-squared minimization approach, yielding accurate results. However, we also observed that the remaining parameters and foregrounds have limited impact on the power spectrum and cannot be constrained. We further analyzed the effects of various factors, such as survey design, instrumental limitations, and data quality, on the parameter estimation. Our simulation is designed to facilitate the assessment of HI intensity mapping experiments, similar to future radio interferometers like SKA.

The dimension of the vector space V is defined as the maximum number of linearly independent vectors within V. These linearly independent vectors form a basis for V. A key theorem states that if a sequence of vectors $\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\}$ is linearly independent, then the dimension of the sequence's vector space is equal to n, and the sequence itself is a basis for that space. This note proves a similar statement but for sequences of matrices. Specifically, it is shown that if a sequence of matrices $\{A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n\}$ has a sequence of vectors $\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\}$ such that each vector is in the nullspace of its corresponding matrix, then the sequence of matrices is linearly independent, and the sequence itself is a basis for that space.

Recommender systems are widely used to mitigate the information overload issue by suggesting relevant items to users. However, these systems face the problem of sparsity, where their performance is significantly impaired by the scarcity of user-item interaction data. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework that integrates multiple data sources, including user-generated content on social media platforms, to predict user preferences. Our approach leverages the semantic information from social media feeds and models user behavior as a continuous time process to gather insights from a limited number of social media data. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on a real-world dataset, which show its superiority over existing techniques.

The freeness property, a concept developed by Voiculescu, can be extended to random matrices with weak or strong asymptotic freeness. We demonstrate that certain matrix ensembles exhibiting eigenvalue fluctuations converging to a specific density, such as independent and identically distributed GUE matrices or the sum of a constant number of GUE matrices, exhibit weak asymptotic freeness. Additionally, we show that certain large random matrix models, such as heavy-tailed matrices or matrices with a specific trace constraint, exhibit strong asymptotic freeness.

This paper presents a monitoring approach for real-time systems based on Metric Interval Temporal Logic, allowing for efficient online detection of predefined patterns within systems that operate in real-time. We demonstrate the practical application of this method in two monitoring tools, showcasing their ability to detect unusual behavior in embedded controllers and network devices that adhere to the IEEE-802.1Qav standard.

The isospin violation in the $D_s^+$ decay to a meson-meson pair, specifically $\pi^0\eta$, is investigated where transition isospin violation dominates over loop corrections. To determine the isospin violation, a comparison is made with the measured $D_s^+$ decay to a $\pi^0\eta$ and the analogous $D^+$ decay to the same meson pair.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera, a part of the Very Large Telescope Interferometer, employs four key optical functions: an image splitter, a beam combiner, a fold mirror, and a pick-off mirror. Utilizing the telescope's native optics, the camera's images are then captured by a 4 Megapixel CMOS sensor, which is subsequently analyzed by the telescope's control software to determine various optical parameters. These parameters are then utilized to calculate the telescope's optical path differences and other relevant data points needed for the alignment process of the GRAVITY instrument.

We develop a novel approximation algorithm for the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problem. Specifically, we show that for any given ε and δ values in the range (0, 1], and a maximum allowable deviation τ ≥ 0, this problem can be solved with an efficient parameterized approximation scheme that runs in n^O(1/(εδ)^2) time, providing a solution no more than (1 + ε) times the optimal value, and containing at most (1 + δ) times the optimal number of suppliers, and with at most τ times the optimal total cost.

This paper examines the hyper order of entire solutions to the equations $f(p_e)^{(k)}}(z)=\exp(Dz)$ and $f(p_{\delta}^{(k)})(z)=\exp(D\ln(1+e^{\lambda z}))$, where $k$ and $\lambda$ are complex numbers, and $D$ is a non-zero real number. It is found that the hyper order of entire solutions to the first equation is less than $\frac{1}{|k|}+\varepsilon$, and for the second equation, it is less than $\frac{1}{|\lambda|}+\varepsilon$.

We investigate solving polynomial linear systems with errors, given that some of the system's components contain measurement errors. Our approach leverages the Wielandt minimization technique to derive a method for obtaining approximate solutions with specific error properties. The number of function evaluations required by our method can be high, with the worst-case scenario involving an exponential increase in computations for certain error scenarios, although we also provide a variant that demands only a linear number of computations, albeit with less stringent error guarantees.

We've developed a theoretical framework for one-dimensional quantum systems that exhibit parity symmetry, allowing us to categorize and systematically construct multi-photon emissions with specific polarization properties. By applying this approach to an array of linear antennas, we've shown that it accurately predicts previously calculated emission patterns and identifies new emission possibilities.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been developed. This equation of state, expressed in terms of the modified Dieterici model, allows for the derivation of multiple thermodynamic properties. Furthermore, the equation of state has been used to determine the polarizability of alkali metals and the scattering cross-sections of their gases.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons are investigated in a medium with chiral imbalance. By utilizing a effective Lagrangian derived from QED for massless fermions, the mass spectrum and form factors of ρ and ω mesons are calculated. Furthermore, the effect of chiral chemical potential on their dispersion relations is analyzed. The findings indicate that the presence of a chiral chemical potential significantly alters the mass spectrum and dispersion relations of these vector mesons.

We present an efficient algorithm that achieves nearly linear time complexity for estimating the diameter of a distributed network, given that it contains a limited number of malicious nodes. Our analysis shows that the algorithm remains reliable even when up to one-eighth of the network's nodes act maliciously. This result is based on previous work that assumed a much lower level of network deception, and we improve upon it by significantly increasing the tolerated number of malicious nodes. We also offer an improved version of the original algorithm that allows for a tighter estimate of the network diameter while still providing robustness against a quarter of malicious nodes.

In numerical relativity simulations that include complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be resolved to generate stable, physically acceptable spacetime configurations. A novel approach for resolving the Hamiltonian constraint in arbitrary, curved spacetimes has been developed, and its effectiveness will be demonstrated through several examples, including a black hole that forms in a specific type of matter called scalar field and a spinning, massive star surrounded by an accretion disk.

The JUNO experiment is an enhanced neutrino observatory based in China, primarily designed to identify the neutrino mass ordering. By utilizing a large, 20-kt LCMS and 3,000 PMT array, it boasts exceptional energy and angle resolutions for neutrino interactions. With a planned data collection duration of 6 years, starting in 2023, it aims to provide conclusive evidence of the neutrino mass ordering. Additionally, the experiment offers substantial research opportunities in other areas, such as precision physics and physics beyond the standard model.

In practical scenarios, long sequence time-series forecasting holds significant value in multiple industries such as weather prediction, stock market analysis, and power consumption forecasting. However, extending time series beyond 24 hours becomes increasingly difficult due to reduced predictability. Existing approaches face challenges in scaling beyond this limit, often resorting to simplified models or combining them with empirical methods. In contrast, we propose a novel framework that leverages recurrent neural networks in conjunction with a spatial correlation module to forecast long sequences up to 90 days with high accuracy. In our experiments, our framework surpasses state-of-the-art models for long-term forecasting, and we also introduce a new dataset for spatial correlation analysis, namely the UKTT dataset.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes are impaired by atmospheric distortion due to differential dispersion, affecting measurements of objects across the sky. The use of an Atmospheric Dispersion Corrector (ADC) mitigates this distortion, but its own light pollution poses a challenge for calibration. We have developed a new method to determine the point spread function (PSF) of an ADC even when the telescope is pointed at the Sun, which is the most difficult scenario. The method combines data from two specific wavelengths to accurately calculate the Sun's PSF. This calibration has been used to investigate the effects of the ADC on the Shandong 1m telescope's images of the Sun.

We explore knowledge distillation as a means to enhance general-purpose ranking models. A novel distillation framework is proposed to transfer knowledge from a strong ranking model to a set of specialized models, each designed for a specific ranking task. The framework relies on a database of artificial, naturally-occurring examples, which are used to define task-specific loss functions and guide the distillation process. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is demonstrated through experiments involving the distillation of a commercial general-purpose ranking model to achieve competitive performance on several targeted ranking tasks.

The near-zero-frequency component of an ultralight bosonic dark matter signal stands out due to its unique characteristics, enabling detection beyond conventional limits. In this analysis, an interrogation laser is employed to enhance the test mass's interaction with dark matter, resulting in a noticeable signal at zero frequency. Traditional frequency modulation techniques fall short in capturing this effect, prompting the development of a new method utilizing the laser's residual phase modulation sidebands. Simulation results indicate that combining test masses with different characteristics can significantly boost detection capabilities, potentially surpassing current limits by several orders of magnitude.

This study examines the uniqueness of solutions for an inverse problem involving a Radon measure and its low-frequency Fourier components.  A key aspect is characterizing the uniqueness of solutions in this inverse problem, which is contingent upon the number of given low-frequency Fourier components.  Furthermore, this work establishes a criterion for identifying the minimal number of required low-frequency components, which is determined by the dimension of a specific convex subset.

P4 is a language used to write switch software, with a compiler that translates programs into hardware-specific code. However, the current compiler only optimizes programs that fit within a predetermined memory limit, failing to utilize available hardware resources when programs exceed this limit. We present a new compiler, P4Flex, which can write optimized instructions during the compilation process, based on the target hardware's specifications and predicted program output. P4Flex includes three main components: a memory predictor, a program analyzer, and an optimizer. The predictor identifies the maximum memory required by a program, the analyzer checks if the program's resources can be reduced, and the optimizer modifies the program to minimize data usage and hazards. P4Flex can handle various programs, including those with multiple tables, and can run on different hardware models.

In numerical simulations of fluid dynamics, the vector transport equation is crucial, and its solution requires significant precision, especially in boundary value problems. A novel approach involves using a function space of higher order than the equation's differential order, enabling more accurate solutions. This paper adapts the space to be compatible with the equation's differential operator, and subsequently develops a corresponding finite element method. A key aspect is the construction of a compatible operator on a triangular mesh, and a corresponding numerical scheme. Several tests confirm the proposed method's high accuracy and efficiency.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked both excitement and unease due to concerns about its ethical implications. This unease stems from previously overlooked issues that have only become apparent in retrospect. This paper identifies several critical, yet understudied ethical considerations associated with deep learning. We then conduct a comprehensive review of existing research to determine the current state of knowledge on these issues. Ultimately, we highlight promising areas for future investigation and outline essential steps for scientists to address these emerging ethical dilemmas proactively.

This letter reports on an observation of an excited $B_c^+$ state, denoted as $B_c^*(5840)^+$, which was initially suggested in 2014 by the LHCb collaboration. The collaboration's findings are based on a study of proton-proton collisions that were recorded by the ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. The observed data show a $B_c^+$ state with a mass of 5841.10 $\pm$ 0.22 $\pm$ 0.3 MeV/c$^2$ and a width of 16.9 $\pm$ 5.5 $\pm$ 3.2 MeV/c$^2$, where the uncertainties represent different sources of error.

We introduce a new class of energy-preserving numerical methods, called Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs), which are derived from generating functions in multistep problems. These methods are shown to be implicit Runge-Kutta-Nystr\"om schemes with specific properties, allowing for a more efficient implementation that directly computes energy values. Some examples and theoretical proofs of stability and convergence are provided.

This paper introduces an innovative method to enhance the training of neural networks using local critic networks, specifically designed for layer group updates. By utilizing these critic networks, our algorithm seeks to optimize the parameter tensors of the network, arranged in predetermined groups, by minimizing the gradient of the loss function along the corresponding matrix principal axes. The algorithm's efficiency is further improved by integrating momentum-based updates, both for the network layers and the critic networks. The results demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms current best practices, including the popular SGD and Adam optimizers, in various benchmark tests.

We investigate a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system that exhibits chaotic dynamics. In the absence of dissipation, some of its basins display non-Wada characteristics. Introducing a minimal level of dissipation causes all basins to transform into Wada basins. This finding is expanded upon by demonstrating that in a particular type of three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system, essentially all basins can be non-Wada, and that dissipation can result in a transition to Wada basins for an infinitely large number of times.

We've developed a theoretical model suggesting that a specific type of lepton interaction can result in a long-lasting, propagating state with a considerable distance between its birth and disappearance points, which could be within reach of current or future particle physics experiments.

Human action understanding in complex videos necessitates the capture of multiple
interconnected temporal structures at various scales. Current methods, however, often
fail to identify and model these multiple structures due to their focus on a single
global sequence. In response, we introduce the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN), a
model designed to capture multiple structures within a video by iteratively learning
from previous structures and adapting its attention mechanism at each scale. In contrast
to existing approaches, HAN's attention mechanism is not only dependent on previous
structures but also on the current one, allowing it to learn from intermediate
intermediate outcomes. We evaluate HAN on the tasks of action localization and unit
action detection and find that it significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art on
these challenges.

This study examines the thermodynamic properties and singularities of Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes across various energy conditions in relation to their electric potential. A key finding indicates the presence of a naked singularity when the horizon radius is less than the square root of half the anti-de Sitter radius. Additionally, the paper explores the thermodynamic stability of the black holes and presents phase transition diagrams.
This article serves as an introduction to a set of lectures on star formation and planet formation, drawing comparisons and contrasts between the processes involved in creating stars and planets.

This study develops a framework for estimating uncertainty in sample data using
information-theoretic metrics like Shannon entropy and mutual information. We adapt these
metrics to categorical and continuous scenarios and demonstrate their applicability to
assessing coverage in active learning. A coverage metric is a measure of how well a set
of unlabeled samples is represented by a model's predictions. We show that this metric
can be calculated by analyzing the conditional probability distribution of unlabeled data
given labeled data. We then investigate how uncertainty changes as new data is
acquired and derive closed-form expressions for specific distribution scenarios. We also
introduce an adaptive query strategy that maximizes coverage and illustrate the benefits
of our framework through experiments on various datasets.

We address the issue of existence and uniqueness for a particular type of differential equation that represents a discontinuous velocity field, which is often used in modeling complex semiconductor factories. The problem is further complicated by a discontinuous right-hand side due to a lack of continuous tracking of individual components. To resolve this challenge, we establish a continuous dependence on initial data and the parameter in question, which in turn enables us to prove the existence and uniqueness of the equation in question.

Cybersecurity is a pressing concern due to the severe consequences of even a minor breach, which can be devastating for a company. As technology advances, cybersecurity challenges evolve, and traditional methods become inadequate. This study presents a novel approach to identifying potential vulnerabilities by converting a cybersecurity problem into a graph theory issue. By applying the maximum flow-minimum cut theorem, we can identify the source of the vulnerability by analyzing the flow distribution and node properties. Our proposed framework is evaluated and validated through experiments on various datasets.

For a finite group G acting on a tree T, we define the Schreier growth gap as the difference between the expected growth rate of the action and the maximum possible growth rate of any group acting on a tree. We show that for any finite group G, there exists a free G-action on a tree with a Schreier growth gap of at least linear, unless G has a specific property in which subgroups are closed under taking intersections with other subgroups.

Locomotion serves multiple purposes for animals, including foraging, self-defense, and social interaction. The variety of locomotion patterns observed across different species suggests that there's no universally effective gait that's suitable for all gait types. This diversity of locomotion also presents challenges for robotic design, as there's no single robot design that can excel in all applications. The choice of robotic design depends on specific goals and conditions. This document provides a comprehensive overview of mobile robots that use different locomotion methods, with a focus on their design principles and key components.

Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In this research, we address the challenge of achieving optimal power transmission under strict constraints in a power grid by formulating it as a mathematical programming problem.
To resolve this issue, we developed a novel, externally guided method utilizing proximal point algorithms within the framework of alternating direction methods of multipliers.
The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations based on standard test networks.

The fundamental objective of both artificial intelligence and physics is to derive general, input-independent truths from specific data sets.  Achieving this goal, however, poses significant challenges under two key conditions: (i) when the target laws governing the system's behavior are complex and not easily formulated; and (ii) when the available measurement data is limited and noisy.  This report examines the current state of machine learning research in the context of these two conditions and highlights potential avenues for future advancement within the framework of predictive modeling and generative learning paradigms.

This analysis presents a comprehensive search for hypothetical heavy, charged particles that persist for a long time, which could be detected in the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. The search focuses on events featuring significant missing energy and one or more isolated, mobile charged particles, as well as pronounced jet and leptonic activity. The study utilizes data collected from 2015-2018, totaling 139 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. To account for various experimental complexities, a statistical method is employed to generate a reliable prediction for observed events. The search results in stringent limits on the cross-sectional production of such particles multiplied by their branching fractions, specifically for a variety of possible lifetimes and various masses ranging from 300 GeV to 6.5 TeV.

A high Purcell factor is crucial for achieving efficient single-photon sources. We demonstrate a solid-state optical cavity for GaAs-based quantum dots by selecting a cavity mode with minimal divergence to the desired quantum dot transition. This choice yields a Purcell factor of approximately 0.98 for the quantum dot's primary transition and enables the analysis of secondary transitions, which could lead to improved single-photon source performance.

Neutron Brillouin scattering offers insights into the vibrational characteristics of a material, particularly its density of states, around its boson peak frequency. A specific technique, incoherent dynamic structure factor extraction from neutron Brillouin scattering data, allows for this information to be obtained with moderate experimental effort. We demonstrate how this method can be utilized to analyze the boson peak of a few glassy materials, such as silicon dioxide and boron oxide, by measuring the vibrational density of states around their boson peaks.

The complexity of modern particle physics demands precise calculations beyond two-loop accuracy for certain processes. Achieving these at the three-loop level, particularly for electroweak or mixed electroweak-QCD corrections, is extremely challenging with conventional methods. Recent breakthroughs using different approaches have shown potential, but these are limited to very specific cases due to computational constraints. This contribution outlines a new strategy to overcome these limitations and highlights promising results that can be derived from it.

In random systems, the scattering matrix relates incident and outgoing wave patterns. We've developed a generalized version of this scattering matrix for any type of wave, which we've applied to two-dimensional non-hermitian systems and found their associated "depletion" states have unique properties.

Recent studies of the Milky Way's spiral arms have been hindered by a lack of reliable data on the Galaxy's central region due to dust obscuration. We have developed a new method to identify the Galaxy's central structure by analyzing the distribution of 6.7 kHz maser sources. Compared to earlier research, our findings show a more accurate representation of the Galaxy's central structure. Notably, we observe a symmetry between the Near Arm and the Far Arm in the Galaxy's central region, and we propose that this symmetry could indicate a spiral pattern with a pitch angle of approximately 10 degrees.

Multi-objective optimization techniques can efficiently generate a diverse set of solutions, but their effectiveness heavily relies on the quality of their surrogate model. In contrast, quality diversity, which searches for diverse and well-performing solutions, often outperforms multi-objective optimization due to its ability to exploit rich environmental information. This paper presents a novel approach, multi-objective quality diversity, which integrates the benefits of both quality diversity and multi-objective optimization. It achieves this by defining a surrogate model that restricts generated solutions to maintain diversity while maximizing their fitness levels. This model is based on a multi-objective formulation that balances two objectives: similarity to existing solutions and fitness. This approach is demonstrated on a simulated benchmark and a real-world robotics challenge, outperforming a multi-objective optimization method in both scenarios.

We explore the computational complexity of the Stable Roommates problem under various constraints, specifically when the preferences are restricted to additive or symmetric valuations. It's known that under general additive preferences, finding a stable matching is an NP-hard task. However, we show that when preferences are additive over three items or symmetric, it's possible to efficiently find a stable matching. This result extends the previous finding by Czumaj and Stobbe that stable matchings could be efficiently computed under symmetric preferences, but only for a limited number of agents.

We have developed a theory to describe the valley Hall effect under static strain in two-dimensional materials like graphene and moire superlattices. By incorporating an effective mass valence force, our model allows for the determination of the valley Hall conductivity via the strain-induced pseudo-Orbitz force. This influence, however, is limited to regions where the effective mass is anisotropic. Our findings demonstrate that both basal and in-plane strains can induce a Valley Hall response, whereas the latter also generates a Valley and Orbital Hall interaction. This strain-to-current mechanism is most pronounced in moire superlattices, where the presence of an additional Orbital Hall effect and tunable Valley Hall effect offers promising applications for valley-based quantum computation and electronic transport.

We establish that the class of all metric spaces, partitioned by their respective Gromov--Hausdorff distances, forms a topological space. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the class of all bounded metric spaces, partitioned by their respective Gromov--Hausdorff distances, also forms a topological space.

This research presents a novel mm-wave microstrip-fed patch antenna designed for integration in planar arrays. The proposed antenna features a unique structure with a slotted circular microstrip patch coupled to a circular cavity resonator via a microstrip feedline. The design enables simple adjustment of the substrate's microstrip parameters to achieve the desired resonant frequency. The antenna's circular geometry facilitates the development of a compact planar array consisting of concentric rings of identical elements. The design's mm-wave capability, specifically within the 28 GHz frequency band, is demonstrated along with the presentation of the antenna's key performance metrics.

A new generation of quantum computers is being developed to outperform conventional supercomputers. However, current quantum devices are limited by decoherence, which can be addressed using topological error correction through the employment of topological codes and quantum gadgets. By combining these approaches, we have developed a framework to numerically analyze the performance of error correcting algorithms at a finite temperature. Our method allows us to efficiently simulate the evolution of these systems and extract key metrics, such as the quantum harmonic mean life, for several established topological codes. Our findings indicate that the performance of these codes can be significantly enhanced through the application of quantum gadgets, and that the most effective method depends on the specific conditions.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging quantum effects, but these benefits are limited when quantum states are constrained by noise. In this context, we examine how to apply quantum metrology to interferometry, specifically with states confined by noise, using multiple weak measurements. Our findings indicate that, even under such conditions, multiple weak measurements can still improve precision in interferometry, achieving a higher power signal than a single weak measurement, provided that certain requirements are met.

Our study examined the suppression of hadrons, particularly those carrying a substantial fraction of the quark's momentum, in Au+Au collisions relative to p+p collisions at 200 GeV. Additionally, we investigated the anisotropic flow of these same hadrons in both collision systems. Utilizing the PYTHIA 6.4 and PHOPOS event generator for p+p, and PYTHIA 6.4 for p+p and gluon-schizrods, we found that the measured hadron suppression and anisotropic flow phenomena are largely reproduced by the model, with the exception of certain low-momentum hadrons.

In digital-analog quantum computing, a method is presented for efficiently simulating fermionic systems using qubits arranged in a specific nanowire-like connectivity pattern. This connectivity structure is found to be optimal for a broad class of fermionic systems, whereas other digital-analog topologies are shown to be less efficient in this context. Furthermore, a general approach is provided to determine the minimum connectivity required for digital-analog simulation of given physical system Hamiltonians.

Recent studies have demonstrated that initializing networks with complex, well-structured representations as the starting point can significantly enhance optimization efficiency and generalization performance. This work delves into the underlying mechanisms through which these initialized components, which we term 'preembodiments,' facilitate improved results. Our analysis reveals that preembodiments can be viewed as both a form of domain knowledge and a means of regularizing the learning process. Furthermore, we identify a critical distinction between components that convey meaningful information and those that do not, and we propose the concept of 'focalability' to capture this essence. Through the lens of focalability, we are able to provide a more nuanced understanding of the properties influencing the effectiveness of preembodiments.
